questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical Kubernetes hardening: securityContext at both pod and container levels, probes that reflect real app health, and a deterministic rolling update trigger. It also checks how to verify and rollback in a live system.

## Key Concepts
- PodSecurityContext and Container SecurityContext
- Probes: readiness vs liveness
- Rolling updates via PodTemplate changes (image digest annotation)
- Verification and rollback workflows

## Code Example
```yaml
# Patch sketch (showing key fields)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: worker
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        kubernetes.io/change-cause: 'security-hardening'
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: your/image:tag
        securityContext:
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 80
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Security hardening of container runtimes and correctness of patching deployments are critical in real-world CKAD tasks.

## Key Concepts
- SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities drop
- Probes: readiness and liveness on /healthz
- Deployment strategy: RollingUpdate for zero-downtime upgrades
- Validation: load testing, rollout status, and rollback workflow

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: portal
  namespace: secure-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: portal
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: portal
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 10001
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 2
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
          timeoutSeconds: 2
```

- How would you adjust if the app requires a limited capability set?
- How would you implement canary rollouts and monitor for regression?

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace operational hardening: config-driven behavior, rolling restarts, health checks, lifecycle hooks, and disruption budgets in CKAD context.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven behavior with pod template checksum for rolling restarts
- Tail/log ingestion from a PVC-backed path
- Probes: readiness /healthz, liveness /livez
- Resource requests/limits and lifecycle preStop
- PodDisruptionBudget to guarantee minimum healthy pods

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-processor
  namespace: audit
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<checksum-from-configmap>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: processor
        image: myrepo/log-processor:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/stream
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: log-stream-pvc
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate rolling restarts trigger on ConfigMap updates?
- How would you simulate load and verify throughput vs. reliability?
- How would you rollback to a previous ConfigMap or image version?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD ability to compose a small, namespace-scoped verification workflow that touches ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, and network policy.

## Key Concepts
- Deployment with InitContainer
- ConfigMap-based allowlist
- Secret-based credentials and TLS sidecar
- PVC-mounted /secrets and lightweight parsing with jq/yq
- Readiness/Liveness probes and per-namespace NetworkPolicy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: compliance-api-creds
  namespace: default
data:
  token: <base64>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: secret-allowlist
  namespace: default
data:
  allowed_keys: |
    tls.key
    tls.crt
    creds
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secret-compliance-checker
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: secret-compliance-checker
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache jq curl && wget -O - https://github.com/yq-dev/yq/releases/latest/download/yq_linux_amd64 -O /usr/local/bin/yq && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/yq"]
      containers:
        - name: checker
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "./check.sh"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: secrets
              mountPath: /secrets
      volumes:
        - name: secrets
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: secret-storage
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale and test this in a real cluster?
- What are risks with mounting Secrets in /secrets and how to mitigate?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design per-namespace automation with ConfigMaps and Secrets, while keeping logs in PVC and restricting egress.

## Key Concepts
- CKAD: CronJob, ConfigMap, Secret, PVC, NetworkPolicy, readiness/liveness probes
- Namespace-scoped automation and centralized scanner integration
- RBAC implications and failure modes

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-scan-cron
  namespace: example-ns
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
          containers:
          - name: trigger
            image: curlimages/curl:8.0
            command: ["sh", "-c", "curl -sS -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $(API_TOKEN)' http://image-scan.local/api/v1/scan?namespace=example-ns --data '{\"ns\":\"example-ns\"}'"]
            env:
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: image-scan-token
                  key: token
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: image-scan-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          serviceAccountName: image-scan-sa
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle failure backoff if the scanner is unreachable?
- What metrics would you expose to ensure cadence fidelity and detect drift?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This CKAD-level question tests comprehensive Kubernetes skills by requiring a complete ETL pipeline implementation with production-ready features including security, reliability, and observability.

## Key Concepts
- **CronJob Management**: Scheduling, concurrency control, and failure handling policies
- **Security Context**: Non-root execution and least privilege principles
- **Volume Management**: Secret, ConfigMap, and PVC mounting strategies
- **Health Monitoring**: Readiness and liveness probes for application reliability
- **Lifecycle Management**: PreStop hooks for graceful shutdown
- **High Availability**: PodDisruptionBudget for maintenance safety

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-processor
  namespace: etl
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 600
  backoffLimit: 3
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
          serviceAccountName: etl-runner
          volumes:
          - name: db-creds
            secret:
              secretName: db-creds
          - name: etl-config
            configMap:
              name: etl-config
          - name: etl-output
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: etl-output
          containers:
          - name: processor
            image: your-processor-image:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: db-creds
              mountPath: /etc/creds
              readOnly: true
            - name: etl-config
              mountPath: /etc/etl/config
              readOnly: true
            - name: etl-output
              mountPath: /data
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses practical CKAD-level skills in CronJobs, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and job lifecycle management, including verification and rollback strategies.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob and Job resources using the batch/v1 API
- ConfigMap volume mounts for configuration and script files
- Secret injection as environment variables
- CronJob policies: concurrencyPolicy, backoffLimit, and successfulJobsHistoryLimit

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: db-backfill
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  backoffLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: db-backfill
            image: postgres:15-alpine
            env:
            - name: PGHOST
              value: db.analytics.svc.cluster.local
            - name: PGPORT
              value: "5432"
            - name: PGUSER
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: username
            - name: PGPASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: password
            command:
            - psql
            - -f
            - /scripts/backfill.sql
            volumeMounts:
            - name: scripts
              mountPath: /scripts
          volumes:
          - name: scripts
            configMap:
              name: backfill-scripts
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Verification Steps
1. Apply the manifest: `kubectl apply -f db-backfill-cronjob.yaml`
2. Verify creation: `kubectl get cronjob db-backfill -n analytics`
3. Check resource details: `kubectl describe cronjob db-backfill -n analytics`
4. View scheduled jobs: `kubectl get jobs -n analytics --watch`
5. Inspect pod logs: `kubectl logs <pod-name> -n analytics`

## Rollback Steps
1. Immediate: `kubectl delete cronjob db-backfill -n analytics`
2. Restore previous version: `kubectl apply -f db-backfill-cronjob.yaml.backup`
3. Suspend job temporarily: `kubectl patch cronjob db-backfill -n analytics -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'`

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design production-ready batch workloads in Kubernetes, including secure configuration management, job lifecycle controls, and deployment strategies for config-driven restarts.

## Key Concepts
- **concurrencyPolicy: Forbid** - Prevents overlapping job executions, ensuring data consistency
- **backoffLimit: 3** - Limits retry attempts for failed pods before marking the job as failed
- **ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400** - Auto-cleansup completed jobs after 24 hours
- **successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3** - Retains recent successful job history for debugging/auditing
- **checksum annotation** - Triggers pod recreation when ConfigMap/Secret changes (requires script to generate hash)
- **envFrom** - Mounts all ConfigMap/Secret values as environment variables without explicit key mapping

## Verification Under Simulated Load
1. **Test concurrency**: Trigger manual job while another runs - should fail with "Cannot determine if job needs to be started"
2. **Test failure handling**: Set invalid config, verify backoff retries 3 times
3. **Test cleanup**: Check completed jobs are removed after 24h TTL

## Verification On Config Change
1. Update ConfigMap: `kubectl apply -f analytics-config.yaml`
2. Verify annotation checksum updates in next job
3. Confirm new pod picks up new environment variables
4. Use `kubectl get pods` to verify new pod creation timestamp

## Why This Matters
This question validates practical Kubernetes skills: namespace-level resource enforcement, working with defaults, and ensuring application reliability through probes and update strategies.

## Key Concepts
- **LimitRange**: Applies default requests/limits to containers without explicit resources. The `defaultRequest` sets what gets requested if not specified; `default` sets the limit.
- **ResourceQuota**: Hard caps preventing namespace resource exhaustion. Tracks usage against hard limits.
- **readinessProbe**: Ensures traffic reaches only ready pods. Uses `/health` HTTP endpoint on port 8080.
- **RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0**: Ensures zero-downtime updates by keeping all old pods running until new ones are ready.

## Verification Under Load
Apply quota/limits first, then patch the deployment. Verify pods receive defaults via `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath`. Under load, confirm quota usage updates and readiness probes correctly gate traffic. The rolling update strategy ensures zero downtime during config changes.

## Rollback
Use `kubectl rollout undo` to revert to previous revision. With `maxUnavailable: 0`, rollback is also zero-downtime. Check revision history with `kubectl rollout history`.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD proficiency across namespace-scoped automation, ConfigMap manipulation, InitContainers, and secure egress controls in real-world migration workflows.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scoped to a namespace with per-namespace behavior
- InitContainer to install tooling (yq) and prepare environment
- ConfigMap-driven migration plan and idempotent updates
- PVC-backed logs and a Secret-backed external POST
- Readiness/Liveness probes for resilient Jobs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to the migration portal

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: per-namespace CronJob migrating ConfigMaps
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: config-migrate
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  schedule: "0 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: migrate-sa
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache go && go install github.com/mikefarah/yq@latest"]
          containers:
          - name: migrate
            image: my-registry/config-migrate:latest
            envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: migration-api
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotent migrations across runs?
- How would you handle partial failures or large numbers of ConfigMaps?
- What monitoring would you add to detect drift or failures?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a per-namespace config pipeline that validates and applies manifests safely inside the cluster while coordinating with a central portal. It exercises InitContainers, in-cluster validation, ConfigMaps/Secrets usage, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace resource provisioning from a PVC
- InitContainer tooling bootstrap (kubectl, yq)
- In-cluster manifest validation via kubectl dry-run
- Runtime config with ConfigMap (BATCH_SIZE)
- Secrets for external portals and TLS cert rotation
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: config-sync
data:
  BATCH_SIZE: "50"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-syncer
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl kubectl yq"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
      containers:
        - name: watcher
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 30; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
      volumes:
        - name: config
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-pvc
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test failure modes if a manifest is invalid after initial processing?
- What changes would you make to scale this for many namespaces?

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD basics: ConfigMap-driven content, Pod specs with probes, RBAC-lite concepts via namespace policies, and basic networking isolation.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap as volume source for static content
- Pod readiness/liveness probes
- Resource requests/limits
- ConfigMap-driven rolling updates via annotation
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: site-content
data:
  index.html: |-
    <html><body>Hello</body></html>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-site
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: static-site
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        site-content-hash: "<hash>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: site-content
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: site-content
        configMap:
          name: site-content
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate updating the site content without full redeploys?
- What are the trade-offs of using a ConfigMap for large HTML content?
